'''''Senecio tamoides''''', also known as '''Canary creeper''',<ref name="zfd">{{cite web
 | url = http://www.zimbabweflora.co.zw/cult/species.php?species_id=161400
 | title = ''Senecio deltoideus'' Less.
 | access-date = 2008-04-14
 | last = Hyde
 | first = Mark
 |author2=Bart Wursten
 | work = Flora of Zimbabwe
}}</ref> is a [[vine|climbing]] member of the genus ''[[Senecio]]'' of the family [[Asteraceae]] that is native to [[Southern Africa]].<ref name="zf">{{cite web
 | url = http://www.zimbabweflora.co.zw/speciesdata/species.php?species_id=161400
 | title = ''Senecio tamoides'' DC.
 | access-date = 2008-04-14
 | last = Hyde
 | first = Mark
 |author2=Bart Wursten
 | work = Flora of Zimbabwe: Cultivated plants
}}</ref> It is used as an [[ornamental plant]] for its showy yellow, daisy-like flowers in late autumn through to winter.<ref>[https://plantinfo.co.za/plant/senecio-tamoides/ Senecio tamoides (Canary creeper)] by Plantinfo</ref><ref name="plantnet"/> Other names for the plant include '''golden shower vine''',<ref>''Sunset Western Garden Book,'' 1995:606–607</ref> '''false grapevine''',<ref>{{cite book |last1=Murrell |first1=Z.E |title=Vascular Plant Taxonomy |date=2010 |publisher=Kendall Hunt Publishing Company}}</ref> and '''parlor ivy'''.<ref>[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/senecio_tamoides.htm Senecio tamoides DC.] Weeds of Australia. Identic Pty Ltd. Retrieved 27 February 2023. </ref> 

==Description==
[[File:Senecio tamoides leaves.jpg|thumb|left|[[Grapevine]]-like leaves]]
It is a fast-growing,<ref name="plantza">[http://pza.sanbi.org/senecio-tamoides Senecio tamoides DC.] by Cheris Viljoen from PlantZAfrica.com</ref> mostly evergreen, perennial climber with semi-succulent stems and leaves<ref name="plantnet"/>
that creeps along the ground or twines several meters into the trees to reach the sunlit [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] where it can flower.<ref name="zf"/> It grows up to a height of {{convert|2|m|ft}} to {{convert|4|m|ft}} tall, though it can be as much as {{convert|10|m|ft}} tall in the right conditions.<ref name="plantza"/><ref name="plantnet"/><ref>[https://apps.lucidcentral.org/plants_se_nsw/text/entities/senecio_tamoides.htm Senecio tamoides] by Betty Wood, Plants of South Eastern New South Wales, Lucid Central</ref><ref name="easy">{{cite book
 | last = Pienaar 
 | first = Kristo
 | title = Gardening with Indigenous Plants: Easy to Grow Southern African Plants
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=UIuW4WTbAPYC
 | access-date = 2008-04-14
 | year = 2003
 | publisher = Struik
 | isbn = 1-86872-392-5
 | pages = 96 pages
 | chapter = Climbers
 | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=UIuW4WTbAPYC&pg=PA80
}}</ref> 

===Stems and leaves===
Its stems are slender, {{convert|3|cm|in}} to {{convert|4|cm|in}} in diameter, usually purplish, semi-[[succulent]] and [[Trichome|hairless]] that have a clear and sticky [[exudate]].<ref name="RFK">{{cite web |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/rainforest/text/entities/Senecio_tamoides.htm |title=''Senecio tamoides'' |author1=F.A.Zich |author2=B.P.M.Hyland |author3=T.Whiffen |author4=R.A.Kerrigan |author2-link=Bernard Hyland |year=2020 |website=[[Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants]] Edition 8 (RFK8) |publisher=Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research (CANBR), [[Australian Government]] |access-date=29 June 2021}}</ref>

Leaves are bright green, [[palmate]]ly lobed with purple [[Venation (botany)|venation]], shaped like many [[hedera|ivy]]<ref name="easy"/> with broad, oval and fleshy surfaces, {{convert|4|cm|in}} long and {{convert|7|cm|in}} wide, coarsely toothed edges, leaf stalks {{convert|2|cm|in}} to {{convert|5|cm|in}} long.<ref name="plantnet"/>

===Flowers===
[[File:Senecio tamoides inflorescences.jpg|thumb|left|Close up of flowers]]
Its [[inflorescence]] is many-headed,<ref name="plantnet"/> bright yellow,<ref name="easy"/> and the [[raceme]] grows to have a flat top. The [[Pseudanthium|flower heads]] are cylindrical, about {{convert|3|mm|in}} in diameter; surrounded with a whorl of five to seven [[bract]]s, {{convert|6|mm|in}} to {{convert|7|mm|in}} long which are surrounded by two to four smaller bracts or bracteoles.<ref name="plantnet">{{cite web
 | url = http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Senecio~tamoides
 | title = PlantNET ''Senecio tamoides'' DC.
 | access-date = 2008-04-14
 | author = National Herbarium of New South Wales
 | author-link = National Herbarium of New South Wales
 | work = New South Wales FloraOnline
 | publisher = [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney]]
}}</ref>  Flowers are [[cinnamon]]-scented that generally appear from mid autumn to winter.<ref name="plantza"/><ref name= shoot>[https://www.shootgardening.co.uk/plant/senecio-tamoides Senecio tamoides (Canary creeper)] by Shoot Gardening</ref> In [[New South Wales]], it flowers in winter. In [[Western Australia]], it flowers between April and May.<ref>[http://www.herbiguide.com.au/Descriptions/hg_Canary_Creeper.htm Canary Creeper, Senecio tamoides DC.] Collated by HerbiGuide. Retrieved May 14, 2023.</ref><ref>[https://eflora.library.sydney.edu.au/taxon/senecio-tamoides *Senecio tamoides DC.] eFlora, 5th Edition of the Flora of the Sydney Region. Retrieved May 14, 2023.</ref>

Three to six ray [[floret]]s; each [[ligule]] approximately {{convert|1|cm|in}} long; ten to twelve disc florets, {{convert|12|mm|in}} to {{convert|15|mm|in}} long.<ref name="plantnet"/> When cultivated in the gardens of the National Museums of Kenya, it has orange florets.<ref name="aluka">{{cite web
 | url = http://www.aluka.org/action/showMetadata?doi=10.5555/AL.AP.FLORA.FTEA006390&pgs=
 | title = Entry for ''SENECIO tamoides'' DC. [family COMPOSITAE]
 | access-date = 2008-04-14
 | author = Aluka
 | author-link = Aluka
 | work = African Plants
 | publisher = Ithaka Harbors, Inc
 | archive-date = 2013-08-01
 | archive-url = https://archive.today/20130801230146/http://www.aluka.org/action/showMetadata?doi=10.5555/AL.AP.FLORA.FTEA006390&pgs=
 | url-status = dead
 }}</ref>

[[Achenes]] about {{convert|2|mm|in}} long, and not hairy; [[Pappus (flower structure)|pappus]] {{convert|6|mm|in}} to {{convert|7|mm|in}} long.<ref name="plantnet"/>
It grows easily from stem cuttings.<ref name="easy"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Seneciotamoides.jpg|thumb|In its natural habitat]]
It is native to southern Africa where it occurs from coastal [[Eastern Cape]] in [[South Africa]] to eastern [[Zimbabwe]], as well as in parts of the forests in [[KwaZulu-Natal]] and areas along the escarpment, including the [[bushveld]] savanna.<ref name = library/><ref>{{cite web |last=Viljoen |first=Cheris |title=''Senecio tamoides'' DC. |url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantqrs/senectam.htm |publisher=PlantZAfrica.com |access-date=11 July 2013 |archive-date=26 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170426234617/http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantqrs/senectam.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> It grows along evergreen forest margins at altitudes of {{convert|300|m|ft}} to {{convert|1900|m|ft}}<ref name="zf"/> and in moist gullies.<ref name="plantnet"/> The plant has been introduced to [[Southeast Brazil]], [[Colombia]], [[Eritrea]], [[Ethiopia]], [[Guatemala]], [[Mauritius]], [[Queensland]] and [[Réunion]].<ref>[https://colplanta.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:247873-1 Senecio tamoides DC.] Useful plants of Colombia from [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]]. Retrieved 2 July 2022.</ref>

===Invasiveness===
In Australia, it is [[Adventive plant|sparingly found]] in moist gullies in [[Sydney]], the [[North Coast (New South Wales)|North Coast]] and [[South Coast (New South Wales)|South Coast]] of New South Wales, and southeast [[Queensland]], after [[escaped plant|escaping]] from the garden as an ornamental plant due to its seeds being dispersed by wind and parts of its stems being spread in disposed garden waste. 

It is a species of concern in south-eastern Queensland, where it was ranked in a list that contains 100 most invasive species in the region. As such, the plant is listed on a few local weed lists in south-eastern Queensland. It is a pest plant in [[Redland Shire]], an invasive plant in [[Gold Coast City]], an unwelcome species in [[Burnett Shire]], a significant non-declared pest plant in [[Maroochy Shire]], and an unwanted species in [[Caboolture Shire]].<ref>[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/senecio_tamoides.htm Senecio tamoides DC.] by Weeds of Australia - Biosecurity Queensland Edition</ref> These reports, however, may have incorrectly applied the ''S. tamoides'' name to ''Senecio angulatus''.<ref>{{cite web
 | url =https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/senecio_angulatus.htm
 | title = Senecio angulatus L. f.
 | access-date = 2020-02-08
 | author = Weeds of Australia (Biosecurity Queensland Edition)
 | publisher = [[Queensland Government]]
}}</ref> Further, ''[[Atlas of Living Australia]]'' has misapplied ''S. tamoides'' for its ''D. odorata'' observations in Australia.<ref>[https://biocache.ala.org.au/occurrences/search?q=lsid%3Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fid.biodiversity.org.au%2Fnode%2Fapni%2F2887441&qualityProfile=ALA&qc=&wkt=MULTIPOLYGON(((150.82031249999997+-33.56318738128773,150.82031249999997%20-34.15618362669792,151.446533203125%20-34.15618362669792,151.446533203125%20-33.56318738128773,150.82031249999997%20-33.56318738128773)))#tab_recordsView  Occurrence records of Senecio tamoides.] Atlas of Living Australia.</ref>

==Similar species==
In [[Australia]], ''Senecio tamoides'' has been misapplied and is usually considered to be ''[[Senecio angulatus]]'' since the two species bear a resemblance, though ''S. tamoides'' (Canary creeper) has leaves that are lighter greened, more ivy or grapevine-like, less glossier and more toothed.<ref name="fbaf-back">{{cite web
 | url = http://florabase.calm.wa.gov.au/search/current/20665
 | title = ''Senecio angulatus'' L.f.
 | access-date = 2008-03-31
 | author = Western Australian Herbarium
 | author-link = Western Australian Herbarium
 | date = 2007-09-11
 | work = FloraBase
 | publisher = [[Government of Western Australia]]
 | archive-date = 2011-05-24
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110524202744/http://florabase.calm.wa.gov.au/search/current/20665
 | url-status = dead
 }}</ref> Moreover, Canary creeper has [[petal]]s that are slightly more elongated, about 10 mm long, compared to those of ''S. angulatus'', which are 6–9 mm long.<ref>[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/senecio_angulatus.htm Senecio angulatus L. f.] Environmental Weeds of Australia</ref> ''[[Delairea odorata]]'' (formerly ''Senecio mikanioides''), a related vine in the [[Senecioneae]] tribe, is also similar looking, but features small ear-shaped appendages at the base of the stalks of the leaves and flowers that lack obvious petals, whereas both ''S. angulatus'' and ''S. tamoides'' have daisy-like flowers with several petals. Unlike ''S. angulatus'', which is more of a scrambler, ''S. tamoides'' and ''Delairea'' grow like typical vines where they intertwine and attach themselves on objects as they climb.

Despite its similarities to the aforementioned species, [[OneZoom]] indicates that ''S. tamoides'' is most closely related to other ''Senecio'' species, including ''[[Senecio keniophytum]]''.<ref>{{cite web 
 |title=Senecio lancidentatus 
 |url=https://www.onezoom.org/life/@Senecio_lancidentatus=7609369?otthome=%40Senecio_tamoides%3D7609833 
 |website=OneZoom Tree of Life Explorer 
 |publisher=OneZoom 
 |date=2026 
 |access-date=2026-03-29 
}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Senecio tamoides flower.jpg|thumb|240px|Potted houseplant]]
It is a fairly drought-tolerant, fast-growing garden plant that grows in well-drained soil towards a wall or fence, and may need some regular [[plant food]] for robust growth and abundant flowering. It needs moderate watering until it becomes established in sun to part shade areas.<ref name = library>[https://www.theplantlibrary.co.za/plants/Senecio-tamoides Senecio tamoides] The Plant Library. Retrieved 1 April 2023.</ref> Its long stems require support to climb, such as on a [[Trellis|trellis]] or a [[pergola]]. It can also be allowed to naturally creep through other shrubs or by planting beside a tree, leaving it to ascend by itself. The plant's growing tips should receive full sunshine for the flowers to develop, though the base can tolerate full shade.<ref name="plantza"/>

Although naturally evergreen, it may be [[semi-evergreen|semi-deciduous]] in places that have frosty winters, where it will die back and recover again in spring. It can be [[pruning|pruned]] once in a while to maintain its spread in the garden. It can be grown from seed in spring, or from stem cuttings in summer.<ref name="plantza"/> In Sweden, it is known as ''Sommarmurgröna'' ('summer ivy'), a name that is also interchangeably used for ''[[Delairea odorata]]'', due to the fact that it grows in summer and dies back to the ground in the cold winter.<ref>[https://www.blomsterlandet.se/tips-rad/vaxtinformation/inne/krukvaxter/grona-vaxter/sommarmurgrona/ Sommarmurgröna] Blomsterlandet 2020</ref>

Medicinally, it has been traditionally used to treat [[flatulence]] and [[anthrax]] in cattle.<ref name = library/> Pests include [[aphids]], [[red spider mite]], [[caterpillar]]s and [[whiteflies]], and diseases include [[Rust (fungus)|rust]].<ref name= shoot/>
